newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Thousands march in Hong Kong over disputed islands.
newsitem.headline: Thousands march in Hong Kong over disputed islands.

text.p: Growing outrage over Japan's occupation of the disputed Diaoyu Islands in the East China Sea brought thousands of Hong Kong protesters onto the streets on Sunday in the largest demonstration yet.
"Chinese people should stand up to defend the Diaoyu Islands," the banner-waving protesters chanted as they marched through streets packed with weekend shoppers.
"Down with Japanese militarism," they shouted at a rally in a playground where they burned Japanese flags in the latest of a series of protests to sweep Hong Kong.

More than 3,000 protestors took part in the demonstration provoked by the latest surge of anti-Japanese sentiment, stoked when Tokyo reasserted its claim to the cluster of islands, also claimed by China and Taiwan.
Anger has been building since Japan stationed naval forces in seas surrounding the unpopulated islands after Japanese rightists built a makeshift lighthouse on one of the islands in July.
Hong Kong's predominantly Chinese residents support Beijing's claim to the Diaoyu Islands, located about 300 km (190 miles) west of the Japanese island of Okinawa and known as Senkakus in Japan.
Anti-Japanese sentiment has united people in Hong Kong, China and Taiwan -- galvanising even groups whose political differences usually keep them at loggerheads.

This led to an unusual sight in Hong Kong on Friday when China's mission in the British territory opened its doors to its arch-foes, the Democratic Party. Members handed over a petition urging Beijing to take action against Japan.
The democrats arrived soon after a pro-Beijing group.
Tokyo's recent moves have spurred new fears of Japanese militarism among Hong Kong people, who have not forgotten the brutalities committed by Japan during its occupation of China and Hong Kong.
"Japan, get out of Diaoyu Islands. Japan must apologise", said the placards brandished by protesters, who also sang the Chinese national anthem.
"The Japanese were defeated in World War Two. So the Diaoyu Islands belong to China," said 75-year-old Siu Kwok-chuen, who fought against Japan in the war.
"The Chinese government is too weak. They are not strong enough to stand up to the Japanese."

"This is a business for all Chinese, for the entire family and not just adults. We should instil to children the concept (of defending Chinese territory)," said a man who brought his children to the demonstration.
Activists also on Sunday ran a signature campaign demanding a boycott of Japanese goods on September 18, the anniversary of the 1931 Japanese invasion of China.
Another action group sought funds for a boat trip to the islands to smash the disputed lighthouse.
A wave of nationalist sentiment has mounted in Hong Kong, adding to the politically charged atmosphere ahead of the handover to China in the middle of next year.
